content:
Earlier this year, I swapped my petrol mower for a robotic lawn mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. You simply use your iPhone to manually drive the robot around your garden once, and the system builds a virtual map. Once set up, it automatically mows according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think this system may be more convenient and easier to use for many users.

Automatic camera mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I previously reviewed lies in how each system understands your garden.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base station positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my phone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. It has three built-in cameras that can automatically map out the lawn area, eliminating the need to lay boundary wires underground or install an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process clearly takes much longer. But I think this method may be simpler for people who are less familiar with technology.

To test this idea, my mother, who lives in another state, set up and used the TerraMow V1000 entirely on her own without any help from me. She replied that everything was working properly. Honestly, I was quite skeptical at the time about whether she would have the patience to manually drive the robot along the boundary and then manually mark no-go zones.

The automatic mapping caused a small issue in my front yard. Since there is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's lawn in my map's coverage area.

I solved this by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if there is no clearly visible dividing line between two lawns, extra care is needed during the initial mapping stage.

Seeing the world through the mower's cameras

The TerraMow cameras also support one of my all-time favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to cast this feed to a larger window. I could sit comfortably indoors and watch the mower make its way through the back yard from the mower's perspective.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and sometimes helps explain why it slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 has no similar camera streaming capability.

The two iPhone apps are fairly similar in other respects. Both let you schedule working times, adjust mowing modes, divide zones, mark no-go zones, and remotely control the mower.

Speaking of that last feature, TerraMow has a particularly outstanding design. In addition to the traditional left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a one-handed joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone in a normal posture and use your thumb to steer the mower.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the primary purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run entirely on schedule without any human intervention. But TerraMow's joystick is very handy for tidying up missed spots.

Sometimes it almost feels like controlling the robot with telekinesis (and it's quite satisfying). I can hold my iPhone by my side, and with just a slight movement of my thumb, the machine goes wherever I want it to.

All robotic lawn mower apps should emulate this style of control.

More aggressive mowing performance

For me, the TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was also noticeably louder while operating.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow noisy, but the difference between the two is very obvious. The Anthbot can run extremely quietly — even if it's mowing at night with its headlights on, it's easy to forget it's still running.

Since TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably, so scheduling daytime mowing becomes all the more important.

The V1000 feels solid and sturdy out of the box, and it's also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a garage with the product to cover the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage must be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow operates reliably and consistently. I've relied on it for several weeks in a row and never had to do any routine mowing myself.

When smart mapping becomes too smart

The same kind of visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. Saving these changes after each mowing session takes some time, during which you can't do anything else in the app.

After several days of heavy rain in a row, I ran into an interesting special situation. Some spots in the garden had collected water, and TerraMow cleverly avoided that area during its next run.

Inside the skipped circular area, the grass grew taller and taller. As time went on, the mower seemed to treat these taller patches as something to keep avoiding, and even after the water had long receded, that patch of grass was never mowed again.

I used the remote control function in the app to manually drive the mower through that patch of tall grass, and the problem was resolved immediately. Once the area looked like normal lawn again, automatic mowing resumed as usual.

Regularly trimming the edges also helps TerraMow handle boundary areas more decisively. If tall grass grows in places with blurry boundaries, it may be mistaken for an obstacle and excluded from the mowing area.

Anthbot's method feels less flexible and relies more on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. This approach requires more upfront work, but at the same time avoids situations where the map "changes its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac review

Having tried both systems, I lean towards recommending the TerraMow camera approach for most people.

For me, underground boundary wires were a non-starter from the beginning, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining an extra piece of hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't perfect. Initial mapping takes longer, hard-to-identify boundaries require manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistakenly treated tall grass as a permanent obstacle.

All of these issues can be resolved. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable and consistent automatic mowing, fun real-time camera footage, and the best manual control experience in a robotic lawn mower app I've seen.

I actually quite enjoy gardening, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this task over to a robot lets me spend more time on landscaping, trimming, and detailed work, while keeping the lawn neat and attractive.

The TerraMow V1000 performs admirably in this regard, enough for me to recommend it, especially for those who want a robotic lawn mower but don't want to dig trenches and lay wires, set up an RTK antenna, or walk the entire garden boundary holding their phone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently available on Amazon and the official website for $999, with a $200 discount coupon available. You can also purchase it through the TerraMow official website.
